title: Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety

reading.body:
Written specifically for clinical safety professionals evaluating AI systems, this paper is aimed at exactly the audience relevant to a healthcare AI audit.

Its intended audience is the distinguishing feature. Rather than writing for AI researchers or for policymakers, it is written for the people who actually sign off on whether a clinical AI system is safe to deploy in a hospital, which shapes what it covers and how it frames the tradeoffs between bias, safety, and clinical benefit.

Published in 2019, it predates the specific demographic-disparity findings on medical language models covered elsewhere in this collection, and does not address large language models specifically since they were not yet in clinical use at the time.

explain_beginner: This paper examines how artificial intelligence systems used in healthcare can develop hidden biases that compromise patient safety. The researchers investigated whether AI tools trained on historical medical data might make unfair or incorrect recommendations for certain groups of patients. Understanding these risks matters because hospitals increasingly rely on AI to help diagnose diseases and guide treatment decisions, so catching bias early prevents harm to vulnerable populations.
explain_business: Healthcare organizations adopting AI tools need formal processes to detect and mitigate algorithmic bias before deployment. This paper provides clinical safety professionals with guidance for auditing AI systems to ensure fair treatment across patient populations and protect against liability. Organizations should implement bias assessment as a standard requirement in their AI procurement and governance processes to maintain safety standards and trust.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of AI bias mechanisms within clinical contexts and their safety implications. They examined how training data characteristics, model development practices, and deployment conditions can introduce or amplify discriminatory patterns in AI decision-making. The study identified that clinical bias emerges through multiple pathways and established a framework for clinical safety professionals to evaluate and audit AI systems for these risks before and during implementation.
